title: Should museums return what they hold?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: The museum's returning the bronzes. It was on the news this morning. All of them, not a loan, actual transfer of ownership.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: I agree with the decision, but I want to be careful about the argument, because the one people usually make is the weak one.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: That they were stolen, so they go back. It's true here, but it stops working the moment something was bought, or given, or dug up by a joint team. And most of the collection is that.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: That an object means more where it came from. A mask in a glass case in a European capital is an artefact. In the place it was made it's still part of something ongoing.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: The counter-argument is access, though, isn't it. Six million people a year walk past those bronzes here.

turns.speaker: Grace
turns.text: Walk past being the operative phrase.

turns.speaker: Grace
turns.text: Nobody's choosing between seeing them here and seeing them there. They're choosing between seeing them and not thinking about it at all.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: That's a bit unfair on the general public.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: Maybe, but the access argument does assume that the people with the strongest claim are the ones least able to travel, and then uses that against them.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Okay. Yes. I hadn't heard it put that way.

points: A museum is transferring ownership of bronzes rather than lending them.
Amara supports the decision but rejects the common argument from theft, because it fails for objects that were bought, given or jointly excavated, which is most collections.
Her stronger argument is contextual meaning: an object in its place of origin remains part of a living culture rather than only an artefact.
Leo raises access, noting six million visitors a year see the objects where they currently are.
Grace replies that the real comparison is not seeing them elsewhere but not engaging at all.
Amara points out the access argument assumes those with the strongest claim are least able to travel, and then uses that fact against them.
